frameworks.name: Return on Time Framework
frameworks.definition: Replace the passive/active income binary with a spectrum measured by return on time (dollars per hour); evaluate activities by their hourly rate relative to personal average.

claims.text: Passive income is a spectrum, not a binary; every person on Earth has a dollars-per-hour rate they generate. The distinction between passive and active is misleading—what matters is measuring return on time (dollars per hour of effort) and comparing it to your personal average.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The binary passive/active framing obscures the real lever—time allocation. When people understand their hourly rate, they can make allocation decisions based on which activities exceed their average rate.

claims.text: To calculate your true hourly rate, divide annual income by 2,000 (forty-hour workweek equivalent) or by approximately 8,000 (total waking hours) to get your true dollars-per-hour return.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Most people mistakenly obsess over finding "quick, easy, low-effort money" (passive income schemes) while under-investing time in activities where they already have high hourly returns, creating opportunity cost by chasing scalability over profitability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to entrepreneurs and income earners at early-to-mid revenue stages
claims.mechanism: The scalability bias ('if it's not scalable, why do it?') causes people to abandon high-return-per-hour activities and spend capital on speculative passive income ventures, which pay off slowly or not at all. Better strategy: maximize active high-rate activities first, then reinvest into multiplication of those activities.
bounded_by: Does not apply once all high-rate activities are saturated and additional capital cannot be deployed into them

claims.text: If an activity generates more per hour than your personal average hourly rate (calculated from last year's total earnings), it is worth doing as many hours as possible until all available hours are allocated to activities at or above that rate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Activity hourly rate > personal average hourly rate
Founder has available hours to allocate
claims.mechanism: Resource allocation to the highest-return activities compounds; prioritizing quantity of high-rate activity over false scalability requirements maximizes compounding.

claims.text: The error Hormozi made (and many founders make) is investing money from active income into passive income schemes rather than reinvesting into multiplication of the proven active income source.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder has validated high-hourly-rate active income
claims.mechanism: Chasing passive income reduces capital available for multiplying proven active income; the capital should flow into leverage (hiring, tooling, marketing) that amplifies the high-return activity's output, not into speculative low-probability passive bets.

claims.text: Most people don't fear trading hours for money—they already do; the semantic confusion is that they expect compensation to be labeled or denoted in hourly units when it is usually not.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The psychological block against hourly thinking is linguistic, not economic. Making the trade explicit (calculating the hourly rate) surfaces the real trade-off and enables rational allocation decisions.

claims.text: In Hormozi's portfolio companies, one specific activity was generating 15 times his personal average hourly rate; he should have prioritized doing as many hours of that activity as possible rather than attempting to scale or delegate it away.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Activity returns > 10x personal average hourly rate
claims.mechanism: High-return-per-hour activities should be maximized before pursuing scalability; the compounding from hours spent at high rates exceeds the long-term payoff from scaling unproven or low-rate activities.

numbers.axis: Activity hourly return relative to personal average

examples.text: Alex Hormozi invested heavily in trying to find passive income schemes—real estate, cryptocurrency, automated systems—hoping to escape time-for-money trades. Meanwhile, he was not scaling the active income activity where he was already highly skilled and profitable, even though that activity was returning 15x his average hourly rate. Only after calculating his true hourly rate did he realize he should have been doing more of that activity and using profits to multiply it (hiring, tooling, marketing) rather than chasing speculative passive plays.

practices.text: Calculate your true hourly rate by dividing annual income by 8,000 (approximate waking hours in a year) or by 2,000 (forty-hour workweek) and use that number as the threshold for evaluating whether an activity is worth your time.

For each activity you do in a month, estimate the total hours and total income generated, calculate the hourly return, and compare it to your personal average. Prioritize maximizing hours on activities that exceed the average; minimize or delegate activities that fall below.

If you have a proven active income source generating above-average returns, reinvest profits into multiplication (hiring, marketing, tooling) for that activity rather than investing into new passive income experiments.
